title_en: AFC/M23 Complains Peace Gains Limited Despite Withdrawal, During UN Visit to Goma
excerpt_en: Goma, North Kivu - April 25, 2026
body_en:
Goma, North Kivu - April 25, 2026

The situation in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo remains tense as the Congo River Alliance and its armed wing, the March 23 Movement, met with a senior United Nations delegation during a field visit to Goma, North Kivu province.

The discussions took place during the visit of James Swan, who is also Head of the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO). He was received on April 24 by AFC/M23 leaders, including Corneille Nangaa and Bertrand Bisimwa.

During the meeting, AFC/M23 representatives presented their assessment of the security and socio-economic situation in areas under their control, claiming improvements in public order and service delivery since their administration took hold.

According to AFC/M23 coordinator Corneille Nangaa, basic services such as healthcare, education, water, electricity, sanitation, and cross-border trade have been restored in territories they control. He also stated that civilian life had stabilized and that infrastructure rehabilitation efforts were underway.

The group further argued that trade corridors and humanitarian access routes through Goma and Bukavu are functioning, despite what they describe as financial and banking restrictions imposed by the central government in Kinshasa.

However, the movement expressed concern over the situation in Uvira, stating that its withdrawal from the area-done, according to them, in “good faith” to support peace efforts-had not produced the expected improvements in security.

Nangaa claimed that civilians in parts of South Kivu remain exposed to violence, including killings, displacement, and destruction of property, blaming government forces and allied armed actors for continued instability.

title: L'Assemblée nationale ratifie des accords clés avec le Rwanda et les États-Unis
excerpt: Kinshasa - April 28, 2026
title_en: DRC National Assembly Ratifies Key Agreements with Rwanda and the United States
excerpt_en: Kinshasa - April 28, 2026
body_en:
Kinshasa - April 28, 2026

The National Assembly of the Democratic Republic of Congo has adopted two major bills ratifying strategic agreements with the United States and Rwanda, following a near-unanimous vote and without substantive debate.

According to official results, 371 of the 372 members present voted in favor, with one vote against and no abstentions.

The two texts were approved after the presentation of the report by the Joint Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defense and Security, and Economic and Financial Affairs. The bills had previously been declared admissible and referred to committee earlier in April.

The agreements were defended before Parliament by Foreign Affairs Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner.

The first agreement establishes a strategic partnership between the DRC and the United States, covering cooperation in key sectors including critical minerals, energy, infrastructure, and security. It also provides for structured collaboration mechanisms and joint monitoring frameworks, while reaffirming respect for national sovereignty.

The second agreement formalizes a peace accord signed on June 27, 2025, between the DRC and Rwanda. It focuses on the cessation of hostilities, respect for territorial integrity, disengagement of forces, and the creation of a joint security coordination mechanism aimed at stabilizing the region.

Lawmakers who participated in earlier discussions stressed the importance of transparency, parliamentary oversight, and strict implementation of commitments, particularly those involving regional security obligations.

title: UN Mission Pushes for Operational Ceasefire Monitoring Mechanism in Eastern DRC
excerpt: Goma, North Kivu - April 27, 2026
title_en: UN Mission Pushes for Operational Ceasefire Monitoring Mechanism in Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: Goma, North Kivu - April 27, 2026
body_en:
Goma, North Kivu - April 27, 2026

Efforts to strengthen ceasefire monitoring in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo have advanced with discussions in Goma between the United Nations and regional verification structures tasked with tracking violations on the ground.

During his visit to North Kivu, the Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General and head of the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), James Swan, met with the leadership of the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism (EJVM+) as well as members of the Joint Intelligence Fusion Center.

The meeting focused on the operationalization of the ceasefire monitoring system established under recent regional and international peace efforts, amid continued clashes between government forces and the Congo River Alliance alongside its armed wing, the March 23 Movement.

According to MONUSCO, the mechanism is intended to verify ceasefire violations and support implementation of agreements reached through ongoing diplomatic processes involving regional and international mediators.

The UN mission indicated its readiness to provide logistical and technical support to initial verification missions, in line with its mandate under Security Council Resolution 2808.

Discussions in Goma follow earlier negotiations held in Montreux, Switzerland, where representatives of the Congolese government and AFC/M23 agreed in principle on the establishment of a strengthened monitoring framework as part of broader peace efforts facilitated by international partners.

MONUSCO welcomed what it described as progress in the peace process, particularly regarding the drafting of protocols on humanitarian access and civilian protection. It urged all parties to maintain engagement in order to finalize and implement the agreements.

title: Kolwezi to Host Mining Tech Summit Focused on Digital Transformation of Mining Sector
excerpt: Kolwezi, Lualaba - April 27, 2026
title_en: Kolwezi to Host Mining Tech Summit Focused on Digital Transformation of Mining Sector
excerpt_en: Kolwezi, Lualaba - April 27, 2026
body_en:
Kolwezi, Lualaba - April 27, 2026

The Democratic Republic of Congo is preparing to host the Mining Tech Summit in Kolwezi, a high-level event aimed at accelerating innovation and digital transformation within the country’s mining industry.

The summit, scheduled for April 30, 2026, will bring together government officials, private sector actors, and technology stakeholders to explore ways of modernizing mining operations through structured technological outsourcing and innovation.

The Minister of Entrepreneurship and Small and Medium Enterprises, Justin Kalumba Mwana-Ngongo, is expected to participate in the event, which is being held under the patronage of Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka.

Organized in Kolwezi at the Convention Village, the summit is coordinated with the Ministry of Digital Economy and the Regulatory Authority for Outsourcing in the Private Sector, alongside public and private partners involved in economic modernization initiatives.

According to organizers, the event will focus on two main priorities: building a structured and competitive technology subcontracting ecosystem to support the mining sector, and aligning regulators, industry players, and innovators around common standards to improve competitiveness and efficiency.

The initiative is part of broader government efforts to integrate Congolese small and medium-sized enterprises into mining value chains, a sector considered central to the country’s economic development.

Officials say the summit is also intended to encourage the emergence of local technological solutions capable of supporting industrial and digital transformation, while reinforcing a regulatory framework that promotes innovation and investment in the mining sector.

title: Opposition Questions U.S.-DRC Migration Deal, Warns of Sovereignty Risks
excerpt: Kinshasa - April 26, 2026
title_en: Opposition Questions U.S.-DRC Migration Deal, Warns of Sovereignty Risks
excerpt_en: Kinshasa - April 26, 2026
body_en:
Kinshasa - April 26, 2026

Opposition leader Delly Sessanga has strongly criticized a reported agreement between the United States and the Democratic Republic of Congo allowing Kinshasa to receive migrants deported from U.S. territory, warning that the arrangement risks turning the country into what he described as a “dumping ground” for foreign migration policies.

The remarks come after reports of a bilateral understanding under which the DRC would temporarily host migrants expelled from the United States, including individuals from third countries, before their return to their countries of origin.

Sessanga accused the government of undermining national sovereignty and questioned the country’s capacity to manage individuals considered security-sensitive by U.S. authorities.

He argued that the DRC, already facing multiple internal security challenges, lacks the institutional and logistical capacity to effectively monitor and manage such cases. He cited national security institutions including the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the police, and intelligence services, questioning their readiness to handle additional security responsibilities.

The opposition figure also criticized the principle of transferring individuals deemed security risks by highly resourced U.S. agencies to a country with more limited capabilities.

He urged the government to reconsider what he described as a policy that could expose the country to additional instability, stating that solidarity should not come at the expense of sovereignty or national security.

The controversy follows reports that more than 1,100 Afghan nationals-formerly affiliated with U.S. forces during the Afghanistan war-have rejected proposals that could see them relocated to the DRC. The group, currently in transit facilities in Qatar, has expressed concern about security conditions and lack of ties to the country.

title_en: AFC/M23 Questions U.S. Neutrality in DRC Peace Mediation
excerpt_en: May 10, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition has formally raised concerns over what it describes as bias in the ongoing international mediation process in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), in a letter addressed to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
body_en:
May 10, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition has formally raised concerns over what it describes as bias in the ongoing international mediation process in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), in a letter addressed to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

In correspondence dated May 7, 2026, Corneille Nangaa, political coordinator of the Alliance Fleuve Congo/M23 (AFC/M23), criticized the conduct of the peace talks facilitated by the United States alongside Qatar and Togo.

The group accuses the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo of failing to implement commitments made during the Montreux negotiations in April 2026, including the planned release of 317 detainees within ten days.

The AFC/M23 also alleges continued drone strikes and air operations targeting areas under its control, as well as attempted assassinations against its leadership.

Beyond these claims, the movement questions the impartiality of U.S. mediation efforts, arguing that Washington’s engagement with Kinshasa has created an imbalance in the peace process, particularly following recent agreements on critical mineral resources between the two governments.

The group further asserts that its own steps toward de-escalation include withdrawals from several territories, the release of detainees, and cooperation on humanitarian arrangements involving the International Committee of the Red Cross.

However, it claims that the security situation in areas such as Uvira has worsened following its withdrawals, attributing this deterioration to the presence of government-aligned forces and allied armed groups.

The letter was also copied to regional and international mediators, including African Union representatives, Qatari officials, Swiss facilitators, and U.S. special advisors involved in the peace process.

excerpt: Kigali, May 14, 2026 - President Paul Kagame has said Rwanda will not alter its policies despite sanctions imposed by the United States earlier this year, acknowledging the measures as painful but insisting they will not influence the country’s strategic direction.
title_en: Kagame Says Rwanda Will Not Yield Despite US Sanctions Pressure
excerpt_en: Kigali, May 14, 2026 - President Paul Kagame has said Rwanda will not alter its policies despite sanctions imposed by the United States earlier this year, acknowledging the measures as painful but insisting they will not influence the country’s strategic direction.
body_en:
Kigali, May 14, 2026 - President Paul Kagame has said Rwanda will not alter its policies despite sanctions imposed by the United States earlier this year, acknowledging the measures as painful but insisting they will not influence the country’s strategic direction.

Speaking during the Africa CEO Forum held in Kigali, Kagame said the sanctions were designed to cause pressure but argued that complying with external demands would be more costly for Rwanda in the long term. He emphasized that the country would continue pursuing its current course, describing it as a matter of principle and national interest.

The Rwandan president also urged African states to resist external political pressure, criticizing what he described as attempts by powerful countries to influence sovereign decisions. He added that such actions would eventually lose relevance over time.

The remarks come amid heightened tensions following US sanctions announced in March targeting Rwanda’s military leadership over allegations related to instability in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The measures include financial restrictions and visa limitations on senior officials.

Despite growing international pressure, Kagame reaffirmed that Rwanda’s position remains unchanged, framing the situation as part of broader geopolitical competition involving regional security and access to strategic mineral resources in the region.

title: Tshisekedi Defends Constitutional Revision Plans, Cites U.S.-Linked Judicial Reforms
excerpt: Kinshasa, May 7, 2026 - President Félix Tshisekedi has reiterated his intention to revise the Constitution of the Democratic Republic of Congo, linking the initiative to judicial reforms associated with a strategic partnership signed with the United States.
title_en: Tshisekedi Defends Constitutional Revision Plans, Cites U.S.-Linked Judicial Reforms
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, May 7, 2026 - President Félix Tshisekedi has reiterated his intention to revise the Constitution of the Democratic Republic of Congo, linking the initiative to judicial reforms associated with a strategic partnership signed with the United States.
body_en:
Kinshasa, May 7, 2026 - President Félix Tshisekedi has reiterated his intention to revise the Constitution of the Democratic Republic of Congo, linking the initiative to judicial reforms associated with a strategic partnership signed with the United States.

Speaking during a press briefing in Kinshasa, the Head of State stated that certain reforms required under the cooperation framework with Washington would not be possible without constitutional changes, particularly in the justice sector.

Tshisekedi argued that constitutional reflection should not be viewed as controversial if it is aimed at addressing institutional challenges and preparing the country for future generations. He emphasized that such discussions are part of long-term governance planning rather than a violation of democratic principles.

The President also referenced a long-standing political vision attributed to his late father, Étienne Tshisekedi, who had expressed support for constitutional change once the UDPS came to power.

The remarks come as lawmakers continue examining a proposed bill regulating referendums and constitutional amendments, which includes provisions for a constituent assembly while maintaining restrictions on presidential term limits under existing constitutional safeguards.

body_en:
KAMPALA, May 12, 2026 - Félix Tshisekedi and Yoweri Museveni held talks in Kampala focused on the progress of Operation Shujaa, the joint military offensive conducted by Congolese and Ugandan forces against the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) and other armed groups operating in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

The meeting took place against a backdrop of renewed deadly attacks attributed to the ADF in the provinces of North Kivu and Ituri, despite ongoing joint military operations launched in November 2021 by the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and the Uganda People’s Defence Force (UPDF).

During the discussions, Félix Tshisekedi emphasized the importance both countries attach to security and stability in the Great Lakes region, particularly in operational zones where the two armies continue to collaborate closely.

The Congolese president praised the quality of exchanges with his Ugandan counterpart regarding military cooperation, although no detailed assessment of the operation’s results was publicly disclosed.

Operation Shujaa was launched to dismantle insurgent groups affiliated with the Islamic State and the ADF, which have been accused of massacres of civilians, sexual violence, forced recruitment of minors, and the establishment of illegal taxation systems in territories under their influence.

Despite the military campaign and the prolonged state of siege in eastern DRC, attacks continue to affect several localities, particularly in Beni territory in North Kivu and in Mambasa and other areas of Ituri. These areas have become epicenters of ADF activity, with recent assaults reported despite the deployment of Congolese and Ugandan troops.

The persistent insecurity has further worsened the humanitarian situation, triggering population displacement and increasing frustration among local communities who feel abandoned by authorities.

The violence has also drawn reactions from the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), which condemned the attacks against civilians and urged all actors to respect international law.

title: Mukwege Opposes Referendum Plan Without Restoration of Security in Eastern DRC
excerpt: KINSHASA, May 15, 2026 - Nobel Peace Prize laureate Denis Mukwege has criticized the ongoing political debate in the Democratic Republic of Congo regarding the possibility of a constitutional referendum while conflict continues in the eastern provinces of North Kivu and South Kivu.
title_en: Mukwege Opposes Referendum Plan Without Restoration of Security in Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, May 15, 2026 - Nobel Peace Prize laureate Denis Mukwege has criticized the ongoing political debate in the Democratic Republic of Congo regarding the possibility of a constitutional referendum while conflict continues in the eastern provinces of North Kivu and South Kivu.
body_en:
KINSHASA, May 15, 2026 - Nobel Peace Prize laureate Denis Mukwege has criticized the ongoing political debate in the Democratic Republic of Congo regarding the possibility of a constitutional referendum while conflict continues in the eastern provinces of North Kivu and South Kivu.

Reacting to recent remarks by President Félix Tshisekedi, in which he suggested that elections could not be held without restoring peace in the conflict-affected east, Mukwege argued that the same principle should apply to any constitutional referendum.

Speaking in an interview with Africanews, he stated that if electoral processes are deemed impossible due to insecurity in the two provinces, then any referendum should also be postponed until all citizens, including those in conflict zones, are able to fully participate.

Mukwege emphasized that democratic legitimacy requires equal participation across the national territory, warning against decisions that could exclude populations affected by ongoing hostilities.

The activist also criticized the broader international engagement in the eastern DRC crisis, particularly referencing cooperation frameworks involving the United States. He accused external partners of prioritizing access to strategic minerals over tangible improvements in security for local populations.

According to Mukwege, mineral exports continue toward international markets, while the security situation in the east remains unresolved, describing the arrangement as increasingly transactional and exploitative.

His remarks come in the context of intensified fighting in eastern DRC, where armed groups, including the AFC/M23 movement, continue to operate in parts of North and South Kivu, despite ongoing regional and international diplomatic initiatives aimed at restoring stability.

Kinshasa, May 19, 2026 - Nobel Peace Prize laureate Denis Mukwege has publicly opposed any attempt to amend the Constitution of the Democratic Republic of Congo in a move that could allow President Félix Tshisekedi to seek a third presidential term.

In a strongly worded two-page statement released on Sunday, May 17, the Congolese doctor and human rights advocate called for strict respect for constitutional provisions, warning against what he described as an “authoritarian drift” in a country already facing political instability and armed conflict in its eastern provinces.

Mukwege argued that discussions surrounding a possible constitutional amendment threaten the foundations of democracy in the DRC.

“The nation seems to be at the mercy of one man, the President of the Republic, and a coalition of political parties seeking to cling to power,” he stated, criticizing what he described as a political system centered on a “cult of personality” rather than democratic alternation.

His remarks come amid growing political debate over potential constitutional reforms, particularly regarding presidential term limits. Although no official proposal has yet been introduced by state institutions, the issue has increasingly dominated political discussions in recent months.

He described the conflict as an “existential threat” to the country and criticized arguments suggesting that insecurity could justify postponing the 2028 elections.

According to Mukwege, if the security situation in North Kivu and South Kivu makes elections impossible, the same conditions would also prevent the organization of a constitutional referendum.

In his message, he expressed continued support for the president’s vision of “stability, peace, and development” and stated that he remains available to serve the Republic in any capacity deemed appropriate by the Head of State.

body_en:
Kinshasa, May 24, 2026 - The political platform “Save the DRC,” associated with former President Joseph Kabila, has welcomed the formation of the Article 64 coalition (C64), a new opposition alliance aimed at defending constitutional order in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The coalition brings together several prominent opposition figures, including Martin Fayulu, Jean-Marc Kabund, and Delly Sessanga, alongside other political actors and civil society groups operating both inside and outside the country.

In a statement, the Kabila-linked movement expressed satisfaction that the newly formed coalition has aligned itself with its long-standing position advocating for the application of Article 64 of the Constitution, which is invoked in cases where citizens are called upon to defend constitutional order against perceived violations.

The platform, which operates in exile, said the emergence of C64 confirms the validity of its political stance regarding governance under the current administration.

“The Save the DRC Movement is delighted to see opposition political parties and social forces finally joining the position it has defended for almost a year,” the statement read, describing the current political situation as requiring urgent constitutional action.

However, the movement also urged the new coalition to broaden its strategy beyond constitutional defense, arguing that the country’s crisis extends deeper than institutional disputes.

It warned against what it described as attempts to amend the Constitution, extend presidential mandates beyond 2028, or open the door to a potential third term for President Félix Tshisekedi.

According to the platform, such developments would represent only surface-level symptoms of broader governance challenges, which it described as including authoritarianism and systemic mismanagement.

title_en: DRC Parliament Divided as Opposition Walks Out Over Referendum Law Debate
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, May 27, 2026 - Tensions flared in the National Assembly on Wednesday as opposition lawmakers staged a walkout during a plenary session dedicated to the examination of a draft law on the organization of referendums in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
body_en:
Kinshasa, May 27, 2026 - Tensions flared in the National Assembly on Wednesday as opposition lawmakers staged a walkout during a plenary session dedicated to the examination of a draft law on the organization of referendums in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The Speaker of the National Assembly, Aimé Boji Sangara, acknowledged the opposition’s withdrawal but insisted that parliamentary work must continue within the constitutional framework and legislative mandate of the institution.

The session focused on the review of the report submitted by the Political, Legal, and Administrative (PAJ) Commission concerning a bill introduced by MP Paul-Gaspard Ngondankoy, a member of the parliamentary majority.

Following a motion for information raised by opposition lawmaker Christian Mwando Nsimba and the subsequent exit of members of the “Ensemble” parliamentary group, Speaker Boji rejected claims that Parliament was attempting to organize a referendum directly within the chamber.

“You are a seasoned parliamentarian, and no one here is organizing a referendum,” he stated, emphasizing that legislators were solely exercising their constitutional duty to debate and legislate.

He explained that the proposed law is intended to establish a legal framework governing the organization of referendums, allowing citizens to express their views on major national issues in accordance with constitutional provisions.

“The purpose of the text being examined today is to provide the Republic with a legal framework enabling our people, the primary sovereign power, to express their views on important issues of national life,” Boji added, stressing that parliamentary debate would continue despite the opposition’s absence.

Earlier in the session, opposition deputies led by Christian Mwando, who also heads the “Ensemble” parliamentary group, left the chamber in protest. They argued that discussions on the referendum bill were taking place in a politically sensitive context marked by insecurity in eastern DRC and alleged foreign involvement alongside the AFC/M23 rebellion.

body_en:
Kinshasa, May 31, 2026 - President Félix Tshisekedi has instructed the Congolese government to conduct a comprehensive review and evaluation of all international agreements signed by the Democratic Republic of Congo in an effort to strengthen their implementation and ensure tangible benefits for the population.

The directive was issued during the 91st meeting of the Council of Ministers held on Friday, May 29, where the Head of State stressed the need for more effective monitoring of bilateral and multilateral partnerships concluded in strategic sectors.

According to the presidency, the review will cover agreements signed in areas including infrastructure, energy, mining, trade, agriculture, health, education, digital technology, and investment.

President Tshisekedi emphasized that these partnerships must generate concrete economic and social outcomes capable of improving living conditions for Congolese citizens.

“In order to fully capitalize on the expected benefits of these partnerships, it is imperative to ensure rigorous monitoring of the effective implementation of the commitments made by our country,” the president stated during the meeting.

The Head of State also recalled previous directives issued during the 70th Council of Ministers meeting in December 2025 regarding the monitoring of strategic agreements concluded with international partners.

To operationalize the initiative, the Prime Minister has been tasked with coordinating a detailed inventory of all agreements signed by the government across various sectors. Each ministry will be required to submit a complete status report on agreements under its authority, whether active, partially implemented, or pending execution.

The process is expected to result in the creation of a centralized and regularly updated strategic matrix designed to monitor, evaluate, and guide the implementation of international commitments.

body_en:
DJIBOUTI, May 9, 2026 - President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh was officially sworn in for a new five-year term on Saturday following his re-election in the April 10 presidential election, where he secured more than 97% of the vote. The inauguration ceremony gathered several African leaders, foreign delegations, and representatives of partner nations in Djibouti City.

In his inaugural address, President Guelleh pledged to continue economic and social reforms aimed at modernizing the country while preserving national stability. He stressed the importance of education, healthcare, youth employment, women’s empowerment, and technological innovation as central pillars of Djibouti’s future development.

“Education is the key to our future,” the president said, while also emphasizing the need to adapt the country’s education system to labor market demands and strengthen opportunities for young people.

The Djiboutian leader further announced plans to expand investments in digital technology and artificial intelligence, while calling for balanced regulation to preserve social cohesion and national values.

On regional and international affairs, President Guelleh reaffirmed Djibouti’s commitment to peace, cooperation, and African integration, stating that climate, health, and economic challenges require collective responses from African nations.

Following the inauguration ceremony, President Guelleh held a series of bilateral meetings with regional leaders and foreign representatives. He participated in a trilateral discussion alongside Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Sudanese Sovereign Council Vice-President Malik Agar, where talks focused on peace, security, and economic integration in the Horn of Africa.

Separate meetings were also held with South Sudanese President Salva Kiir and Yemeni Presidential Council President Rashad al-Alimi to discuss bilateral cooperation and regional stability.

Additional diplomatic talks brought together President Guelleh with Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly, Algerian Senate Speaker Nasri Azzouz, French Minister Catherine Vautrin, China’s Special Envoy Luosung Jiangeu, and United Nations Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa Guang Cong.

excerpt_en: Djibouti, May 2, 2026 - The Republic of Djibouti has been selected to host the next session of the Conference of Ministers of Education of the States and Governments of La Francophonie (CONFEMEN), scheduled for 2028.
body_en:
Djibouti, May 2, 2026 - The Republic of Djibouti has been selected to host the next session of the Conference of Ministers of Education of the States and Governments of La Francophonie (CONFEMEN), scheduled for 2028.

The decision was made during the 61st CONFEMEN session held from April 27 to May 1 in Yaoundé, Cameroon, where member states chose Djibouti following a competitive selection process involving Romania and Gabon.

Officials said the selection reflects renewed confidence in Djibouti’s role within the Francophone education space and recognition of its ongoing commitment to strengthening education systems and promoting Francophone cooperation.

A Djiboutian delegation led by Ayan Osman Abrar, technical advisor to the Minister of Education and national correspondent for CONFEMEN, took part in the deliberations of the session, which brought together education authorities from across member states.

Discussions among participating countries focused on strengthening cooperation in education policy, improving quality standards, and reinforcing solidarity within the Francophone community.

Founded in 1960, CONFEMEN brings together education ministers from 41 Francophone states and governments, meeting every two years to coordinate policies and advance shared educational priorities.

body_en:
Washington, April 20, 2026 - Djibouti has warned of far-reaching and “exceptional” consequences of the current global crisis on African economies, during the IMF-World Bank Spring Meetings held from April 13 to 18 in Washington.

Representing Djibouti, Central Bank Governor Ahmed Osman Ali described the global environment as “unprecedented,” citing the ongoing Middle East tensions and disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz, a critical maritime corridor through which an estimated 20% of global oil flows.

He noted that these disruptions have triggered sharp increases in energy prices, higher maritime transport costs, and widespread supply chain instability, with direct implications for international trade and food systems.

Despite these external pressures, Djibouti reported continued macroeconomic resilience, with growth estimated at 6.5% in 2025 and projected at around 6% in 2026, supported by strong port activity and infrastructure-driven economic performance. Authorities also indicated that inflation remains contained and the banking sector stable.

However, officials cautioned that this resilience remains fragile due to structural vulnerabilities, particularly the country’s heavy reliance on imported food and energy. Rising freight and energy costs are increasingly affecting both businesses and household purchasing power.

Djibouti has responded with a series of emergency measures, including price controls, strategic stock management, prioritisation of essential imports, and targeted support interventions, particularly in the energy sector. A national task force has also been activated to coordinate responses between public and private actors.

During discussions with the IMF Managing Director, the Central Bank Governor described the situation as a “tipping point,” stressing that the intensity of current global shocks is placing significant strain on fiscal stability, particularly through rising fuel import costs and price stabilisation policies that have increased pressure on public finances.

He also highlighted the social dimension of the crisis, noting that food inflation remains particularly severe in a country where households spend a large share of their income on basic consumption needs.

The workshop brought together technical partners and institutional representatives to review the scope, objectives, and implementation challenges of both projects, while also providing a platform for stakeholder input aimed at strengthening inclusive and sustainable execution.

Officials said the session was also designed to explain the functioning of the complaints management mechanism, which will be used to collect feedback, address concerns, and improve project delivery in line with international standards.

Opening the workshop, Project Manager and Director of ICT Development Faycal Khaireh Chirdon highlighted the importance of digital transformation in building a more inclusive and connected society.

He stressed that the government’s approach goes beyond infrastructure development, focusing instead on creating an ecosystem that enables citizens to acquire essential digital skills and participate meaningfully in the digital economy.

Chirdon reaffirmed the government’s commitment to reducing the digital divide in Djibouti, noting that both DFN and EARDIP are central to this objective.

The two initiatives are supported through funding from the World Bank’s International Development Association (IDA), with $10 million allocated to the DFN project and $20 million directed toward EARDIP.

According to officials, the investments are intended to strengthen ICT sector competitiveness, attract private sector participation, and enhance regional digital integration across East Africa.

title_en: Guelleh Overhauls Government in Major Cabinet Reshuffle
excerpt_en: Djibouti, May 17, 2026 - President Ismail Omar Guelleh carried out a significant cabinet reshuffle on Sunday, introducing new ministers, reallocating key portfolios, and dismissing several senior officials in one of the most extensive government reorganizations in recent years.
body_en:
Djibouti, May 17, 2026 - President Ismail Omar Guelleh carried out a significant cabinet reshuffle on Sunday, introducing new ministers, reallocating key portfolios, and dismissing several senior officials in one of the most extensive government reorganizations in recent years.

The changes include the departure of several high-profile figures, notably the Minister of Health Ahmed Robleh Abdilleh, the Minister of Youth and Culture Hibo Moumin Assoweh, and the Minister of Trade and Tourism Mohamed Warsama Dirieh. They have been replaced respectively by Mouna Osman Aden, Fardoussa Moussa Egueh, and Orbis Helaf Orbis, with the latter two joining the government for the first time.

Further exits include Minister Delegate for Decentralization Kassim Haroun and Secretary of State for Sports Hassan Mohamed Kamil. Their positions are now held by Omar Houssein Omar and Fatouma Ali Abdallah.

The reshuffle also triggered a broader reallocation of ministerial responsibilities. Mohamed Abdoulkader Moussa moves from the Environment portfolio to head the Ministry of Communication, responsible for Posts and Telecommunications, replacing Radwan Abdillahi Bahdon. Bahdon, in turn, takes over the expanded Ministry of Agriculture, Water, Fisheries, Livestock, and Marine Resources, while Mohamed Ahmed Awaleh assumes leadership of the Environment Ministry.

title: Djibouti Pushes Ambitious Aquaculture Drive to Boost Food Security and Investment
excerpt: Djibouti, May 12, 2026 - Djibouti has launched an ambitious push to develop its aquaculture sector, with authorities and international partners unveiling plans aimed at transforming fish production, reducing reliance on seafood imports, and creating new economic opportunities.

excerpt_en: Djibouti, May 12, 2026 - Djibouti has launched an ambitious push to develop its aquaculture sector, with authorities and international partners unveiling plans aimed at transforming fish production, reducing reliance on seafood imports, and creating new economic opportunities.
body_en:
Djibouti, May 12, 2026 - Djibouti has launched an ambitious push to develop its aquaculture sector, with authorities and international partners unveiling plans aimed at transforming fish production, reducing reliance on seafood imports, and creating new economic opportunities.

The initiative was presented during a major workshop held Tuesday at the Sheraton Hotel, bringing together government officials, international experts, financial institutions, training centers, and private sector operators. The event was organized by the Ministry of Agriculture, Water, Fisheries, Livestock, and Marine Resources in partnership with the World Bank as part of the country’s broader economic transformation strategy under the national development agenda for 2030.

Opening the meeting, Minister Mohamed Ahmed Awaleh stressed that the objective extends beyond attracting investors, focusing instead on building a complete aquaculture value chain covering production, processing, transport, and commercialization.

The project envisions the establishment of a modern marine aquaculture system inspired by the Norwegian model, including floating fish cages across three strategic coastal zones, notably in Obock and Tadjourah. Authorities estimate that the initiative could eventually generate up to 18,000 tons of fish annually, significantly strengthening the country’s food self-sufficiency.

Plans also include the construction of specialized infrastructure such as live-fish transport vessels, automated feeding systems, a hatchery in the Red Sea region, and a fish processing plant within a free trade zone.

Officials say Djibouti possesses strong natural advantages for the sector, including an extensive coastline, favorable climatic conditions, and positive technical feasibility studies that position the country among Africa’s emerging aquaculture destinations.

However, authorities acknowledged that the sector’s success will depend on major investments in maritime infrastructure, cold-chain logistics, processing facilities, and workforce training. Participants at the workshop highlighted the importance of developing local expertise to ensure the long-term sustainability and competitiveness of the industry.

The initiative builds on discussions launched during the Agribusiness Forum held in June 2025 with support from international partners including the World Bank, the Food and Agriculture Organization, the African Development Bank, and the International Fund for Agricultural Development.

Djibouti, May 14, 2026 - Djibouti has launched a new National Cooling Action Plan aimed at modernizing the country’s cooling infrastructure and improving resilience to rising temperatures, growing energy demand, and public health challenges.

The initiative was officially unveiled by the Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources under the leadership of Minister Yonis Ali Guedi, in partnership with the United Nations Development Programme and the Regional Council for Energy and Environment (RCREEE).

Authorities describe the program as a major step in the country’s energy transition strategy, focusing on the development of sustainable and energy-efficient cooling systems across multiple sectors. The plan covers air conditioning in buildings, food preservation systems, vaccine and medicine storage, hospital infrastructure, and climate-adapted urban planning.

With temperatures continuing to rise and demand for cooling rapidly increasing, officials say the project is designed to protect public health while reducing pressure on the national electricity grid.

The strategy promotes modern technologies and environmentally sustainable solutions, including bioclimatic construction methods, improved thermal insulation, high-efficiency cooling equipment, and greater use of renewable energy sources, particularly solar energy.

Authorities expect the program to deliver significant economic and social benefits. In the energy sector, it is intended to lower electricity consumption and reduce the risk of grid overloads. In healthcare, the plan seeks to improve the storage and preservation of vaccines, medicines, and other sensitive medical supplies.

The initiative is also expected to support the expansion of a modern cold chain system, considered essential for agriculture, fisheries, food distribution, and export activities.

Officials further highlighted the social impact of the project, noting that improved cooling systems could help populations cope with increasingly severe heat waves while providing better protection for vulnerable communities.

Both countries are also engaged in major regional infrastructure projects, including the development of a railway linking Isaka and Kigali to improve cargo transport efficiency.

Bilateral relations are further supported by cooperation frameworks and business and friendship associations that promote collaboration between citizens and private sectors in both countries.

title_en: DRC parliamentary report highlights weaknesses in national security forces
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, 29 April 2026 - A report by the National Assembly of the Democratic Republic of Congo has raised serious concerns over the capacity of the country’s armed forces and allied groups to effectively secure national territory, citing structural and operational shortcomings.
body_en:
Kinshasa, 29 April 2026 - A report by the National Assembly of the Democratic Republic of Congo has raised serious concerns over the capacity of the country’s armed forces and allied groups to effectively secure national territory, citing structural and operational shortcomings.

The findings follow consultations held in December 2025 between the parliamentary committee on defence and security and several key government officials, including ministers responsible for security, defence, finance, public service and mining. The discussions aimed to assess the state of national security amid ongoing conflicts in the eastern regions.

According to the report, the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) face multiple challenges, including indiscipline, outdated equipment and infiltration by hostile elements. These weaknesses have reportedly undermined the military’s ability to respond effectively to armed groups, particularly in North and South Kivu.

Officials also highlighted broader security concerns across the country, including the presence of foreign forces in parts of Tanganyika province and local conflicts in northern regions. Authorities warned that without swift and coordinated action, the situation could deteriorate further, with implications for national stability, governance and economic activity.

The defence minister acknowledged recent investments in military technology, including drones and combat aircraft, but noted that opposing forces have adapted with countermeasures, limiting their effectiveness. He emphasized the need for a comprehensive strategy combining military, diplomatic, intelligence and economic approaches, alongside broader reforms within the security sector.

The report further pointed to governance and financial management challenges. Although significant funds were allocated to the military in 2025, not all resources were fully utilized, and some planned expenditures were not executed. Concerns were also raised over delays in the payment of allowances to deployed soldiers.

The role of the Wazalendo militia alliance was also examined. While these groups are seen by some officials as important partners in territorial defence, the report highlighted issues related to their organization, conduct and oversight. Tensions between the militia and regular forces have reportedly increased in recent months.

Authorities indicated that future plans include maintaining cooperation with local armed groups during ongoing operations, while considering long-term measures such as disarmament, reintegration or potential integration into formal security structures.

The decision was reached during an extraordinary general assembly held on April 26, where party members convened to determine their flagbearer for the upcoming vote.

Ndayishimiye, who came to power in 2020 after winning the presidential election, is now set to seek a second term in office.

Speaking during a recent press conference, Tshisekedi said he had initially considered direct intervention but ultimately concluded that the Congolese army was not sufficiently prepared for such an operation.

The Congolese president also discussed relations with the United States, describing Washington as a close partner and linking that relationship to his government’s willingness to receive migrants under agreements with the United States.

During the press conference, Tshisekedi warned that continued instability in eastern Congo could affect the country’s political future, stating that elections scheduled for 2028 may not take place if the conflict persists.

His remarks come amid ongoing regional and international efforts to restore security and advance political dialogue in eastern DRC.

KINSHASA, Democratic Republic of Congo, May 29, 2026 - American and Swiss diplomatic representatives have reviewed the implementation of commitments made during peace talks between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government and the AFC/M23 movement, raising questions over progress on agreed confidence-building measures.

Representatives of the two sides met in Montreux, Switzerland, in April 2026, where they agreed to observe a ceasefire and facilitate the release of detainees as part of efforts to reduce tensions in eastern DRC. The agreement reportedly included the release of hundreds of prisoners within ten days.

On May 26, US and Swiss envoys traveled to Kinshasa and held discussions with DRC government officials involved in the Montreux process. During the meetings, the delegations reportedly sought updates on the implementation of prisoner releases and the security situation on the ground.

The following day, authorities announced the release of 37 individuals accused of links to AFC/M23. According to information provided during the talks, the broader Montreux framework called for the release of 311 detainees held by the government, while AFC/M23 was expected to facilitate the release of 166 individuals linked to state institutions.

AFC/M23 officials maintain that the movement had already released several government-affiliated detainees, including members of the security forces and their relatives, before the Montreux negotiations took place.

The American and Swiss delegations had planned to continue consultations in Goma but altered their itinerary following reports of an Ebola case in the area. Instead, meetings with AFC/M23 representatives were held in Rubavu, near the DRC-Rwanda border.

Discussions also touched on developments around Rubaya, a strategically important mining center known for its coltan deposits. The area has remained under AFC/M23 control since May 2024 and continues to be a focal point in the conflict.

AFC/M23 officials have indicated their willingness to engage in discussions regarding the future of the area with international stakeholders. Meanwhile, the DRC government continues efforts to reassert authority over Rubaya through diplomatic initiatives and military operations.

body_en:
KINSHASA, Democratic Republic of Congo, May 30, 2026 - Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dr. Denis Mukwege has sharply criticized President Félix Tshisekedi, accusing him of “grave and unforgivable treason” amid growing political tension over proposed constitutional reforms in the DRC.

In a statement issued on May 30, 2026, Mukwege warned that efforts linked to extending presidential mandates risk diverting attention from urgent national challenges, including insecurity in eastern provinces and ongoing public health crises such as Ebola outbreaks.

He argued that political debate within the ruling establishment, particularly within the UDPS party, has increasingly focused on the possibility of constitutional revision to allow for a third presidential term, rather than addressing pressing governance issues.

Mukwege also criticized members of parliament supporting the initiative, suggesting that political incentives and personal benefits were driving backing for the proposal.

According to him, some lawmakers from conflict-affected regions, including Ituri, North Kivu and South Kivu, are among those supporting the initiative, despite ongoing instability in their constituencies.

“The UDPS, which was once a model for the revolution, has become a conduit for conspiracy that is leading our country to destruction,” Mukwege said in his statement.

He urged President Tshisekedi to refocus on constitutional obligations and national stability, warning that history would judge leadership decisions made during the current political debate.

The remarks come after Tshisekedi suggested in early May that constitutional reform could be considered and that he would respect public demand regarding a potential extension of his mandate. He also indicated that the 2027 elections might not proceed as initially scheduled.

body_en:
OTTAWA, Canada, May 27, 2026 - Canada has announced a temporary suspension of entry for travelers from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and South Sudan in response to the ongoing Ebola outbreak affecting parts of East and Central Africa.

The measure, effective for 90 days starting May 27, was confirmed by Public Health Canada as part of efforts to prevent the spread of the virus beyond the continent.

Under the new restrictions, entry is prohibited for nationals of the three affected countries. However, Canadian citizens, permanent residents and foreign nationals who have recently traveled to these countries will still be allowed to enter, provided they undergo a mandatory 21-day quarantine.

The decision follows similar measures announced by other countries. On May 26, the government of the Bahamas imposed a 30-day entry ban on travelers from the same countries, while also introducing enhanced screening and quarantine requirements for individuals who have recently visited affected areas.

Earlier, the United States also introduced a temporary travel restriction of 21 days for individuals coming from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and South Sudan, citing concerns over potential cross-border transmission.

Khartoum, 5 May 2026 - Sudanese authorities have accused the United Arab Emirates and Ethiopia of involvement in recent drone strikes targeting Khartoum International Airport and other strategic locations in the capital, marking a sharp escalation in regional tensions linked to the ongoing conflict.

The accusations followed coordinated aerial attacks that struck the airport, residential neighbourhoods, and military installations including the Signal Corps base in Khartoum Bahri and the Al-Markhiyat training camp in Omdurman.

Sudanese officials stated during a press briefing that they possessed what they described as “conclusive evidence” showing drones involved in the attacks were launched from facilities in Bahir Dar. Military representatives also claimed that technical tracking data linked some of the drones to Emirati ownership and alleged that similar aircraft had previously been used in operations across Blue Nile and Kordofan before one was intercepted near El Obeid earlier this year.

In response to the latest developments, Sudan announced the recall of its ambassador from Addis Ababa for consultations, while officials warned that the country reserved the right to respond to what it described as repeated violations of its sovereignty.

The allegations add further strain to already tense regional relations as Sudan’s conflict increasingly takes on broader geopolitical dimensions amid expanding drone warfare and cross-border accusations.

He also promised improved administration and public services in RSF-controlled areas, including support for wounded fighters and educational assistance for families affected by the conflict.

body_en:
Khartoum, 4 May 2026 - Landmines and unexploded ordnance have killed at least 25 people and injured 52 others in Sudan since the beginning of the year, according to the United Nations Mine Action Service (UNMAS), which warned that the real number of casualties is likely much higher.

The victims recorded between January and March included dozens of children, as growing numbers of displaced civilians return to areas heavily affected by fighting, particularly in Khartoum State. Humanitarian agencies estimate that around 1.8 million people have returned to the capital region after fleeing earlier phases of the conflict.

UNMAS said clearance teams have removed thousands of explosive devices and restored millions of square meters of land for civilian use since the war began in April 2023. However, new minefields and unexploded ordnance continue to be discovered, including in central Khartoum and around infrastructure projects linking Omdurman and Khartoum Bahri.

Both the Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have been accused of laying anti-personnel and anti-vehicle mines across contested territories during the conflict, contributing to a growing humanitarian threat for returning civilians and aid workers.

Mine-clearing operations have also focused on strategic facilities, including Khartoum International Airport, where hundreds of explosive hazards were removed to allow humanitarian flights to resume earlier this year. Additional clearance efforts have targeted homes, schools, hospitals, and farmland in affected communities.

The European Union recently announced additional funding to support mine-action activities in Sudan, as humanitarian organizations continue surveying hazardous areas and expanding explosive-risk awareness programmes for civilians and relief personnel.

body_en:
Khartoum, 2 May 2026 - Sudan’s military ruler, General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, has issued an apology for violence committed by soldiers against medical personnel in hospitals, while also praising health workers for their role in providing information that aided the army’s advance in southern Khartoum.

In a statement from the Sovereignty Council, Burhan acknowledged “harshness” by individual soldiers toward medical staff and commended doctors and health workers for continuing to operate under difficult wartime conditions, as the healthcare system remains severely strained by years of conflict.

The remarks come against the backdrop of a collapsing health infrastructure, with thousands of medical personnel killed or injured and more than 2,000 health facilities destroyed since the outbreak of war in April 2023.

Burhan also claimed that intelligence provided by medical staff contributed to the army’s capture of parts of southern Khartoum, where government forces regained control in May 2025 after intense fighting with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). He denied that the military deliberately targets hospitals, while accusing the RSF of repeated attacks on healthcare facilities.

Humanitarian organizations, however, continue to document widespread assaults on medical infrastructure across the country, underscoring the severe toll the conflict has taken on civilians and essential services.

title: Burhan Announces Internal Political Dialogue to Advance Sudan’s Democratic Transition
excerpt: Khartoum, May 26, 2026 - Sudanese Sovereignty Council Chairman and army commander General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan announced Tuesday that preparations are underway for a broad internal political dialogue aimed at reaching national consensus on completing Sudan’s civilian democratic transition.
title_en: Burhan Announces Internal Political Dialogue to Advance Sudan’s Democratic Transition
excerpt_en: Khartoum, May 26, 2026 - Sudanese Sovereignty Council Chairman and army commander General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan announced Tuesday that preparations are underway for a broad internal political dialogue aimed at reaching national consensus on completing Sudan’s civilian democratic transition.
body_en:
Khartoum, May 26, 2026 - Sudanese Sovereignty Council Chairman and army commander General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan announced Tuesday that preparations are underway for a broad internal political dialogue aimed at reaching national consensus on completing Sudan’s civilian democratic transition.

In an Eid al-Adha address to the nation, Burhan said the proposed dialogue would bring together Sudanese political and social stakeholders inside the country to agree on principles of governance and chart a path toward civilian democratic rule following years of conflict and political turmoil.

“The government of Sudan will provide everything necessary to ensure the success of this dialogue,” Burhan said, adding that participation would be open to national actors “whose hands are not stained with the blood of the Sudanese people.”

He stressed that the process would be conducted entirely within Sudan and would include individuals and groups directly affected by the ongoing crisis and war. Burhan also pledged that the government would commit itself to implementing any agreements reached through the dialogue.

The army chief rejected externally sponsored political initiatives, criticizing conferences held abroad and warning against what he described as foreign-driven agendas or ideological interference in Sudan’s internal affairs.

Sudan has faced deep political instability since October 2021, when Burhan dissolved the civilian-led transitional government established after the 2019 uprising that removed former president Omar al-Bashir. Relations between military authorities and civilian groups deteriorated further before escalating into full-scale war in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

The conflict has since caused a severe humanitarian crisis, widespread displacement, and increasing political fragmentation across the country.

Burhan’s announcement comes amid ongoing international and regional efforts to revive negotiations and establish a framework for ending the war and restoring civilian governance in Sudan.

title_en: Sudanese Political and Civil Leaders Converge in Nairobi to Form Broad Anti-War Civilian Alliance
excerpt_en: Nairobi, May 20, 2026 - A wide delegation of Sudanese political figures, civil society actors, and armed movement representatives has gathered in the Kenyan capital to participate in talks aimed at forming an expanded civilian coalition to end Sudan’s ongoing war.
body_en:
Nairobi, May 20, 2026 - A wide delegation of Sudanese political figures, civil society actors, and armed movement representatives has gathered in the Kenyan capital to participate in talks aimed at forming an expanded civilian coalition to end Sudan’s ongoing war.

The two-day meetings, scheduled for May 22-23, bring together signatories of the “Sudanese Declaration of Principles for Building a New Homeland,” a framework agreement signed in Nairobi in December 2025. The declaration rejects military solutions to the conflict and calls for coordinated pressure on the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), and allied armed groups to commit to a proposed peace roadmap under the Quad mechanism.

According to Mohamed Abdel Rahman, spokesperson for the Sudan Liberation Movement led by Abdul Wahid al-Nur, the discussions will focus on assessing the current political and security situation in Sudan and expanding the principles of the declaration into a broader unified platform.

He said the initiative aims to build the “broadest civilian front” capable of steering the country toward a political settlement and ending the war. However, he noted that participation would exclude certain political forces, including the National Congress Party, the Islamic Movement, and other groups opposed to peaceful resolution efforts.

The delegation includes prominent political leaders such as Dr. Abdalla Hamdok, head of the “Samoud” coalition; Abdul Wahid Mohamed Nur, leader of the SLM; Omar al-Digeir of the Sudanese Congress Party; and Al-Wathiq al-Berier of the National Umma Party. Also present are figures from various opposition blocs, armed movements, professional associations, and civil society organizations.

Other attendees include Yasir Arman of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (Revolutionary Democratic Current), Babiker Faisal of the Unionist Alliance, and leaders from both the Arab Socialist Ba’ath Party - Original and the National Ba’ath Party, alongside representatives of trade unions and professional networks.

The meeting comes amid stalled peace initiatives and intensifying military operations across multiple regions, as competing armed factions continue to fight for territorial control and political leverage.

Ankara, May 22, 2026 - Sudan and Turkey have concluded the 16th session of their Joint Ministerial Economic Committee, agreeing on a series of cooperation projects in agriculture, energy, and mining aimed at strengthening bilateral economic ties and supporting Sudan’s reconstruction efforts.

Minister Ismat Qurashi expressed appreciation for Turkey’s continued support during Sudan’s conflict period, reaffirming Sudan’s commitment to executing the agreed projects in line with shared development priorities. His Turkish counterpart urged the swift implementation of the agreements and called for an increase in bilateral trade, describing economic cooperation as a central pillar of relations between the two countries.

title: Sudan Power Sector Collapses as War Inflicts $3 Billion Damage, Solar Adoption Surges
excerpt: Khartoum, May 18, 2026 - Sudan’s electricity sector has suffered damages estimated at $3 billion since the outbreak of the ongoing conflict, triggering a nationwide shift toward solar energy as households, businesses, and telecommunications operators struggle to cope with a collapsing national grid
title_en: Sudan Power Sector Collapses as War Inflicts $3 Billion Damage, Solar Adoption Surges
excerpt_en: Khartoum, May 18, 2026 - Sudan’s electricity sector has suffered damages estimated at $3 billion since the outbreak of the ongoing conflict, triggering a nationwide shift toward solar energy as households, businesses, and telecommunications operators struggle to cope with a collapsing national grid
body_en:
Khartoum, May 18, 2026 - Sudan’s electricity sector has suffered damages estimated at $3 billion since the outbreak of the ongoing conflict, triggering a nationwide shift toward solar energy as households, businesses, and telecommunications operators struggle to cope with a collapsing national grid and soaring diesel costs, according to a United Nations report released Monday.

The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Sudan said widespread destruction of power generation facilities and transmission infrastructure has forced a rapid, largely unplanned transition to solar energy, despite persistent cost pressures and disrupted supply chains. The country, which benefits from some of the world’s highest solar irradiance levels, has an estimated technical potential of 15 gigawatts (GW) of solar power and 1.5 GW of wind energy. Yet before the war, grid electricity reached only 45% to 60% of the population, leaving rural and remote communities heavily dependent on off-grid solutions.

The report estimated Sudan’s installed solar capacity at about 190 megawatts (MW) by 2025-far below pre-war government ambitions to generate 3,300 MW of renewable energy by 2033, including 2,190 MW from solar sources.

The conflict also derailed state-led programs such as plans to distribute 2.5 million solar home systems to off-grid communities. In their place, private imports of solar equipment surged between 2024 and 2025 as grid failures intensified and fuel prices became increasingly prohibitive.

However, the UNDP warned that the sector remains highly fragile. Because all components-including panels, batteries, and inverters-are imported, the market is heavily exposed to currency depreciation, foreign exchange shortages, and high domestic logistics costs. The report detailed that importation costs through Port Sudan were significantly inflated by internal transport fees, port storage charges, demurrage, and documentation expenses, all of which collectively eroded affordability for end users.

In retail markets across cities such as Atbara, Port Sudan, Dongola, and Khartoum, solar panel prices reached between 218,000 and 255,000 Sudanese pounds for a 590-watt unit in late 2025, while 10-kilowatt lithium batteries were priced above 5 million Sudanese pounds.

Despite rising adoption, regional disparities remain pronounced. Khartoum leads with solar penetration above 7%, followed by Kordofan at around 6% and Darfur at 5%, while eastern and central regions lag at roughly 3%.

The economic consequences of the energy crisis have been severe, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises and agriculture. In Gedaref, farmers reported significant yield declines linked to unreliable power supply. In Blue Nile, diesel scarcity pushed fuel prices to extreme levels, while irrigation systems in White Nile were left idle for extended periods due to fuel shortages.

title: Burhan Rejects Bahrain Mediation Reports, Vows to Eliminate RSF
excerpt: KHARTOUM, May 29, 2026 - Abdel Fattah al-Burhan on Thursday firmly denied reports alleging that consultations had taken place in Bahrain regarding possible dialogue between Sudan and the United Arab Emirates, dismissing claims published by Middle East Eye as entirely false.
title_en: Burhan Rejects Bahrain Mediation Reports, Vows to Eliminate RSF
excerpt_en: KHARTOUM, May 29, 2026 - Abdel Fattah al-Burhan on Thursday firmly denied reports alleging that consultations had taken place in Bahrain regarding possible dialogue between Sudan and the United Arab Emirates, dismissing claims published by Middle East Eye as entirely false.
body_en:
KHARTOUM, May 29, 2026 - Abdel Fattah al-Burhan on Thursday firmly denied reports alleging that consultations had taken place in Bahrain regarding possible dialogue between Sudan and the United Arab Emirates, dismissing claims published by Middle East Eye as entirely false.

Speaking during an Eid al-Adha address to military commanders at the General Command headquarters in Khartoum, Burhan said there had been no discussions in Bahrain and rejected suggestions of indirect mediation efforts involving Abu Dhabi.

“What Middle East Eye reported is completely untrue,” Burhan stated. “The talk of consultations in Bahrain has no basis in truth whatsoever.”

The remarks marked Burhan’s first direct public response to a report published last week claiming that he had expressed conditional openness to talks with the UAE, provided Emirati support for the Rapid Support Forces ceased. The report also suggested that Bahrain was attempting to facilitate contacts between Khartoum and Abu Dhabi.

Burhan’s Gulf tour earlier this month included visits to Saudi Arabia, Oman, and Bahrain, although Sudanese authorities only officially announced his meeting with Bahrain’s king. The Sovereignty Council’s media office had previously issued an indirect rebuttal to the report, stating that Burhan had not recently spoken to any media outlet.

In a strongly worded speech, Burhan reiterated the Sudanese military’s determination to continue the war against the RSF, pledging the complete dismantling of the paramilitary force.

“There will be no RSF militia in Sudan, no Janjaweed from this day on, and no room for any rebel in our country,” he declared.

The Sudanese army chief said military operations were progressing steadily and promised that government forces would eventually retake Darfur “city by city.” He also praised allied armed factions, mobilized fighters, and popular resistance groups supporting the army’s campaign.

body_en:
Kampala, May 4, 2026 - President Yoweri Museveni has presided over the final Cabinet meeting of the outgoing government at State House, marking the formal conclusion of the current executive term and reflecting on what he described as key achievements in Uganda’s economic transformation.

The meeting, which officials described as the “final Cabinet of fishermen meeting,” brought together ministers to wrap up government business ahead of the transition to a new administration phase. Museveni used the occasion to commend the outgoing Cabinet for its role in steering Uganda toward middle-income status.

During the session, the President revisited his 2021 Cabinet formation philosophy, explaining that he deliberately selected what he termed “fishermen” - a reference to ordinary, tested individuals - rather than elite professionals, drawing a comparison to biblical discipleship.

He reiterated that his selection approach was guided by trust in leaders he considered disciplined, non-corrupt, and aligned with government priorities, arguing that such individuals were better suited to implement national development goals.

Following the formal meeting, the President hosted ministers for a farewell luncheon at State House, turning the occasion into a moment of reflection and appreciation for their service.

Museveni praised the Cabinet for its contribution to what he described as Uganda’s economic advancement, particularly the attainment of middle-income status. He cited progress in infrastructure development, energy expansion, and agricultural modernization as key drivers of the country’s improved economic standing.

He also commended the Cabinet Secretariat for ensuring effective coordination of government business and policy implementation throughout the term.

The President said the outgoing administration had operated under the “Securing Your Future” development agenda, which focuses on economic growth and structural transformation.

body_en:
Kampala, April 28, 2026 - Uganda’s central bank has cautioned that the proposed Protection of Sovereignty Bill, 2026 could destabilise the country’s macroeconomic environment by weakening the shilling, reducing foreign investor inflows, and reigniting inflationary pressures if passed in its current form.

Appearing before Parliament’s Joint Committee on Defence and Internal Affairs and Legal and Parliamentary Affairs, the Governor of the Bank of Uganda warned that the legislation risks undermining decades of financial liberalisation that have supported economic growth and stability.

He stressed that while the intention behind strengthening national sovereignty is legitimate, any disruption to capital inflows could have far-reaching consequences on Uganda’s balance of payments position and foreign exchange reserves. He added that reduced inflows would likely lead to currency depreciation, which in turn would increase the cost of imported goods and push inflation above the central bank’s 5% target.

The central bank further cautioned that Uganda’s foreign reserves, estimated at around USD 6 billion, could come under pressure if investor confidence weakens. It noted that recent stability in the shilling has been supported by a balance of payments surplus of approximately $1.5 billion in the last financial year.

According to the bank, any shock to these inflows could force reserve drawdowns, increasing economic vulnerability.

In recent months, the shilling has shown relative resilience, trading in a range of approximately Shs3,650-3,850 per US dollar. It has also remained broadly stable against regional currencies, supported by export earnings, remittances, and development financing.

However, economists warn that this stability remains fragile and highly dependent on continued foreign exchange inflows. A sustained depreciation, they caution, would raise the cost of imports such as fuel, machinery, and pharmaceuticals, feeding into broader inflation across key sectors including manufacturing and transport.

Over time, a weaker currency could also reduce household purchasing power, increase the burden of foreign-denominated debt, and dampen investor appetite for Ugandan assets.

title: Uganda Courts Chinese Capital as Anite Hosts High-Level Investor Delegation
excerpt: Kampala, April 29, 2026 - Uganda has stepped up efforts to attract foreign direct investment, with government officials intensifying engagement with Chinese investors as part of a broader industrialisation strategy.
title_en: Uganda Courts Chinese Capital as Anite Hosts High-Level Investor Delegation
excerpt_en: Kampala, April 29, 2026 - Uganda has stepped up efforts to attract foreign direct investment, with government officials intensifying engagement with Chinese investors as part of a broader industrialisation strategy.
body_en:
Kampala, April 29, 2026 - Uganda has stepped up efforts to attract foreign direct investment, with government officials intensifying engagement with Chinese investors as part of a broader industrialisation strategy.

State Minister for Privatization and Investment Evelyn Anite received a delegation of Chinese investors led by Wendi Shen, President of the Henan Chamber of Commerce, in discussions centred on expanding investment into key sectors of the Ugandan economy.

The visiting delegation is assessing opportunities aligned with Uganda’s development priorities, particularly in manufacturing and value addition, as the country seeks to transition from exporting raw materials to building stronger domestic production capacity.

During the engagement, the minister urged investors to focus on export-oriented industries and strengthen local supply chains, noting that Uganda is actively positioning itself as a competitive manufacturing base in the region.

She highlighted improvements in investment fundamentals, including expanded transport infrastructure, increased electricity generation capacity, and sustained political stability, which government officials say continue to underpin investor confidence.

Uganda’s investment promotion strategy is currently concentrated on high-growth sectors such as minerals and mining, oil and gas, agro-industrialisation, and pharmaceuticals. Authorities argue that these sectors present opportunities not only for capital investment but also for technology transfer, industrial upgrading, and skills development.

The Chinese delegation expressed interest in the country’s economic prospects, with its leader describing Uganda as a promising destination for long-term investment. The group also signalled intentions to mobilise additional investors to explore potential partnerships across priority sectors.

Officials say the engagement reflects strengthening economic ties between Uganda and China, as Kampala positions itself as a regional industrial and investment hub. Increased foreign participation, particularly from China, is expected to support manufacturing growth, expand export capacity, and generate employment opportunities, especially for Uganda’s young and expanding workforce.
