title: DRC and Uganda Conclude Joint Commission Meeting Ahead of Strategic Agreements
excerpt: KAMPALA, May 10, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda on Sunday concluded the 9th session of their Joint Standing Commission in Kampala, paving the way for the signing of six strategic agreements aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation and regional integration.
title_en: DRC and Uganda Conclude Joint Commission Meeting Ahead of Strategic Agreements
excerpt_en: KAMPALA, May 10, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda on Sunday concluded the 9th session of their Joint Standing Commission in Kampala, paving the way for the signing of six strategic agreements aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation and regional integration.
body_en:
KAMPALA, May 10, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda on Sunday concluded the 9th session of their Joint Standing Commission in Kampala, paving the way for the signing of six strategic agreements aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation and regional integration.

Held from May 8 to 10 under the theme “Accelerating Shared Prosperity: Trade, Infrastructure, and Security for Enhanced Regional Stability and Socio-Economic Transformation,” the meeting brought together senior officials from both countries to discuss cooperation in the security, economic, and trade sectors.

At the end of the discussions, ministers from the two countries endorsed a report prepared by technical experts and approved by the secretaries-general of the relevant ministries. The document outlines priority areas of cooperation intended to improve trade flows and strengthen stability along the shared border between the two neighboring states.

The highlight of the meeting will be the signing of six memoranda of understanding scheduled for Monday, May 11, at State House, in the presence of Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni.

The agreements are expected to focus on trade cooperation, partnerships between the National Agency for Export Promotion (ANAPEX) and the Uganda Free Zones and Export Promotions Authority (UFZEPA), tourism development, information and communication technologies, and collaboration in peacetime search and rescue operations.

Both countries also reiterated their commitment to improving cross-border trade infrastructure through the construction of one-stop border posts and modern border markets in Kasindi, Bunagana, and Mahagi.

Congolese Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior and Security, Jacquemain Shabani, who led the Congolese delegation, praised the growing strategic partnership between Kinshasa and Kampala, saying it would contribute to regional stability and economic integration.

The Congolese delegation included several cabinet members, among them the Ministers of Foreign Trade, Foreign Affairs, Agriculture, Hydrocarbons, Infrastructure, Communication, Regional Integration, Tourism, Fisheries and Livestock, and Water Resources and Electricity.

title_en: Museveni Announces 2026-2031 Cabinet, Retains Janet, Drops Kasaija and Gen. Ali

body_en:
Kampala, May 26, 2026 - President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni has unveiled a new Cabinet for the 2026-2031 term, introducing major changes across government, including the removal of long-serving ministers Matia Kasaija and Gen. Moses Ali, while maintaining continuity in several key positions.

The announcement outlines a broad reshuffle affecting economic management, security, and senior government coordination roles, under constitutional provisions governing executive appointments.

Vice President Jessica Rose Epel Alupo retains her position, while Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja also remains in office as Leader of Government Business in Parliament.

Among the most significant changes is the appointment of Henry Musasizi as Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic Development, replacing Matia Kasaija, who does not appear on the new Cabinet list after years in the role.

First Lady Janet Kataaha Museveni retains her position as Minister of Education and Sports, continuing to oversee the sector amid ongoing national reforms in education policy.

In the restructuring of senior leadership, Rebecca Kadaga has been named First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for East African Community Affairs, while Dr. Crispus Walter Kiyonga becomes Second Deputy Prime Minister and Deputy Leader of Government Business in Parliament. Lukia Nakadama has been appointed Third Deputy Prime Minister and Minister without Portfolio.

Within the Office of the President, Babirye Milly Babalanda retains her portfolio, while security oversight remains under Jim Muhwezi. Eng. Jonard Asiimwe has been appointed Minister for Science, Technology and Innovation.

The reshuffle also sees Ruth Nankabirwa and Evelyn Anite moved out of Cabinet roles and appointed as Senior Presidential Advisors, alongside Francis Mwebesa and Hamson Obua, signaling a shift of experienced officials into advisory positions.

body_en:
Kampala, May 23, 2026 - President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni has launched a sharp rebuke against veteran journalist Andrew Mwenda, accusing him of undermining Uganda’s industrialisation strategy, leaking confidential government discussions, and advancing what he described as neo-colonial interests.

In a detailed statement released on social media, the President responded to recent remarks attributed to Mwenda questioning his leadership and judgment, dismissing claims that he is “senile” while defending his continued capacity to lead the country.

“Mr. Mwenda, thank you for declaring me senile and incapable of judging right,” Museveni wrote. “You will, however, discover that at 82, I am still able to defend Uganda and myself with the Bible, the AK-47 and the pen.”

The President’s response expanded into a broader defense of government economic policy, particularly its industrialisation drive and efforts to promote value addition in agriculture and mineral resources.

Museveni accused Mwenda of consistently criticizing local entrepreneurs and innovators while ignoring what he described as successful domestic industrial projects across the country.

He cited several examples of local initiatives, including manufacturing and agricultural ventures, arguing that they demonstrate Uganda’s growing capacity for self-reliant development.

The President also defended state-supported projects such as Kiira Motors Corporation, rejecting criticism over delays and government investment in the automotive initiative.

He further argued that opposition to such projects reflects resistance to Africa’s industrial transformation and a preference for continued dependence on raw material exports.

body_en:
Kampala, May 21, 2026 - Quality Chemical Industries Limited has launched the local production of Hydroxyurea, a key medication used in the treatment of Sickle Cell Disease, marking a significant step in Uganda’s pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity and efforts to improve access to essential medicines.

The drug, locally branded as Sikurea, is produced at the company’s Luzira facility and is expected to reduce painful crises, lower hospital admissions, and improve the quality of life for patients living with sickle cell disease.

The production line was officially commissioned by the Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary, Dr Diana Atwine, who described the initiative as a breakthrough in strengthening Uganda’s healthcare system and expanding access to affordable treatment.

“By launching this local manufacturing capacity, Uganda has crossed yet another threshold. What we are launching today is not just medicine on the market, but a transformation in the lives of our people,” she said.

title_en: New Speaker Jacob Oboth-Oboth Faces High Expectations Amid Parliament Reform Promises
excerpt_en: Kampala, May 26, 2026 - Newly elected Speaker of Parliament Jacob Oboth-Oboth has pledged wide-ranging reforms aimed at restoring transparency, accountability, and public trust in Uganda’s legislature, even as analysts question his ability to confront entrenched political interests.
body_en:
Kampala, May 26, 2026 - Newly elected Speaker of Parliament Jacob Oboth-Oboth has pledged wide-ranging reforms aimed at restoring transparency, accountability, and public trust in Uganda’s legislature, even as analysts question his ability to confront entrenched political interests.

Upon assuming office, Oboth-Oboth outlined a seven-point reform agenda focused on zero tolerance for corruption, stronger accountability systems, evidence-based legislative debate, results-oriented budgeting, improved public engagement, and enhanced oversight of public funds.

He also promised to open up Parliament’s operations to the public and strengthen media engagement as part of efforts to rebuild institutional credibility.

However, political analysts and critics remain skeptical about the feasibility of his reform ambitions within an institution long accused of being shaped by patronage networks and executive influence.

Veteran MP Ibrahim Ssemujju Nganda warned that expectations of radical change may be unrealistic, arguing that the Speaker operates within deeply entrenched parliamentary structures.

He cautioned that meaningful reform would depend on how Oboth-Oboth manages key institutional processes, particularly the Appointments Committee and budget-related decisions.

Ssemujju also raised concerns about long-standing issues such as discretionary spending and parliamentary allowances, suggesting that structural changes would be required to meaningfully curb corruption.

Some lawmakers, however, have urged patience and a more measured assessment of the new Speaker’s performance.
